docs.title: Global Index on Responsible AI Handbook
Introduction
docs.text: The Global Index on Responsible AI is a global measurement initiative that tracks country progress toward responsible AI, mapping policies, regulatory frameworks, and civil society engagement. It serves as an evidence-based tool to inform global debates and policy recommendations, drive government action, and encourage private sector alignment with responsible AI principles.

docs.title: What does the index measure?
docs.text: The Index assesses countries’ commitments and practices to ensure that the design, development, deployment, adoption, and oversight of artificial intelligence are ethical, rights-respecting, inclusive, and aligned with democratic values and principles. It does so by evaluating the existence of government frameworks and their implementation, government-led initiatives where such frameworks are absent, and civil society engagement — across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and Use of AI in Public Service Delivery.

docs.title: Index Structure
docs.text:
The Global Index on Responsible AI is structured around dimensions that align with human rights-based standards and democratic principles.

Each dimension is measured through indicators that capture core components of Responsible AI, based on the operationalisation of the UNESCO Recommendation.

To provide a comprehensive picture, the indicators are grouped into three categories:

  • government frameworks and practices indicators, which assess the existence, scope, and implementation of government frameworks and initiatives, including implementing activities, actions taken in the absence of frameworks, and instances of government misuse;
  • civil society engagement indicators, which capture the involvement of civil society organisations in shaping Responsible AI; and
  • country context indicators, which account for the broader enabling conditions relevant Responsible AI.

Each dimension is built from indicators, some drawn from primary data and others from secondary data, whose results are then aggregated to produce the overall score of the Global Index.

docs.title: Who should use this Handbook
docs.text:
The Handbook is intended for use by all members of the GIRAI research network. This includes:

  • country researchers, who complete the GIRAI questionnaires and draft country summaries;
  • country coordinators, who report for their own country while also overseeing the work of other researchers within their region, reviewing all answers, and identifying relevant regional repositories;
  • regional supervisors, from the Global Center on AI Governance (GCG) or partner institutions, who monitor coordinators’ work and spot-check submissions; and
  • global reviewers, responsible AI and policy experts who conduct the final validation of all approved answers.

Each group plays a distinct but complementary role in building a robust and credible Index.

docs.title: Dimensions and Indicators of the Global Index on Responsible AI
docs.text:
The five dimensions of the Global Index, along with their indicators, are:

  1. Inclusion and Diversity Definition: The value of promoting different backgrounds, groups, perspectives, and identities to ensure equitable participation, representation and belonging for all in the design, development, and deployment of AI.

    1. Gender Equality (primary)
    2. Children's Rights (primary)
    3. Rights of Persons with Disabilities (secondary)
    4. Cultural and Linguistic Diversity (primary)
    5. CSO Engagement on Inclusion and Diversity (primary)
    6. Equality (secondary)

  2. Ethics and Sustainability Definition: The principles guiding right, fair, and responsible human actions, and decisions, ensuring a practice of meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

    1. Fairness and Non Discrimination (primary)
    2. Transparency and Explainability (primary)
    3. Human Oversight and Determination (primary)
    4. Environmental Impact (primary)
    5. CSO Engagement on Ethics and Sustainability (primary)
    6. Environmental Performance Index (secondary)/
    7. Ethics (secondary)

docs.title: CSO Engagement on Ethics and Sustainability
docs.text:
DefinitionWhy Measure this IndicatorWhat to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • To safeguard people's rights effectively, active civic participation is essential in ensuring accountability, amplifying marginalised voices, and representing the public interest in AI governance processes. In this regard, civil society organisations (CSOs) working in the field of artificial intelligence play a crucial role in actively shaping policies, implementing projects, raising public awareness, lobbying for policy formulation and implementation, and holding the government to account.

  • According to the United Nations, “a civil society organisation (CSO) or non-governmental organisation (NGO) is any non-profit, voluntary citizens’ group which is organised on a local, national or international level” . These organisations focus on specific issues of public interest, such as human rights, poverty alleviation, inclusion, and inequality. The EU notes that “civil society refers to all forms of social action carried out by individuals or groups who are neither connected to nor managed by state authorities”, while CSOs are institutionalised or formal organisations “whose members serve the general interest through a democratic process and which plays the role of mediator between public authorities and citizens”.

  • CSOs operate through a variety of structures, including as charities, faith-based organisations, think tanks and research centres, trade unions, community groups, online networks, and social and recreational clubs. In the AI context, the defining quality for a CSO is that the non-profit organisation engages in policy influencing, public awareness, research, knowledge production, advisory, advocacy or any other activity geared towards responsible development and deployment of AI.

CSOs play a critical, sometimes outsized role, in advancing responsible AI practices and policies. Data from the 2024 edition of the Global Index on Responsible AI identified more than 400 CSOs working to advance responsible AI across 19 thematic areas including gender equality, children's rights, and cultural and linguistic diversity. Evidence of CSO engagement in these areas fill a crucial gap and offer a holistic assessment of the responsible AI ecosystem globally, given that in some contexts — such as Africa — CSO activities often surpass government-led efforts in responsible AI.

The questionnaire for this indicator asks researchers to document evidence of CSO activities across all indicators (primary and secondary) in the Ethics and Sustainability dimension: Fairness and non-discrimination, Transparency and Explainability, Human Oversight and Determination, and Environmental Impact. Researchers should therefore consider both the breadth of the evidence of initiatives as well as how well such evidence covers all the indicators. There are 6 CSO initiative types in the questionnaire:

  • Participation in public policy formulation, implementation, M\&E: as part of advisory councils, partnerships with state, independent observers, participating in parliamentary hearings
  • Litigation or legal action.
  • Capacity building and collaboration
  • Public engagement & awareness: conferences, public awareness events/campaigns, public consultations
  • Knowledge generation: research, technical reports.
  • Developing ethical guidelines, standards, and best practices

You are to provide one evidence per initiative type and indicate which indicator the evidence covers. It is very likely that initiatives are more concentrated on one indicator than others – this is fine, but we encourage researchers to ensure, where evidence is available, that each indicator has at least one evidence of a CSO initiative addressing it. Initiatives must be either ongoing or have taken place during the study timeframe (November 1, 2023 – September 30, 2025).

You should only provide evidence that shows country-level engagement of CSO initiatives. Evidence from international CSOs are relevant, only if the initiative addresses your country's context and actual participation in the initiative from local partners could be demonstrated — this includes country chapters of international CSOs. A relevant example here is Amnesty International, an international CSO operating in more than 150 countries, which has led a campaign to ban facial recognition technologies in the Hyderabad city of India.

Examples below are provided by initiative type:

Participation in public policy formulation, implementation, M\&E: as part of advisory councils, partnerships with state, independent observers, participating in parliamentary hearings:

KICTANet Kenya is a multistakeholder think tank working on digital policy and regulation. In January 2025, it co-convened with the Kenyan Ministry of ICT & Digital Economy, a multistakeholder workshop on the Kenya AI Statement of Principles. The workshop fed into Kenya’s national AI Strategy, and emphasised core principles relating to the ethics & sustainability dimension, including human-centred design and accountability, transparency and public trust, and environmental sustainability.

Litigation or legal action.

In June 2025, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) in the USA filed an amicus in the New Jersey Supreme Court in the case brought against the State of New Jersey by Mr Miles. The EFF urged the court to require prosecutors to disclose how facial-recognition tools work (source code, error rates etc) to defendants identified via Facial recognition technologies; a process that aims to strengthen transparency and explainability in AI systems.

Capacity building and collaboration

The Alan Turing Institute in the UK regularly offers training courses and workshops, and has published a publicly accessible playbook (2024) on transparency and explainability in AI.

Public engagement & awareness: conferences, public awareness events/campaigns, public consultations:

The U.S.-based Algorithmic Justice League recognises AI’s potential for perpetuating different forms of discrimination as a result of bias and works to raise public awareness using a combination of art and research as well as to “equip advocates with resources to bolster campaigns, build the voice and choice of the most impacted communities, and galvanize researchers, policymakers, and industry practitioners to prevent AI harms.” Alongside its ongoing research and conferences, the organisation runs the multi-stakeholder project Community Reporting of Algorithmic System Harms which allows individuals to report harms from algorithms and seek redress through the community.

Knowledge generation: research, technical reports.

In December 2024, Friends of the Earth Ireland in partnership with Prof. Hannah Daly at the University College Cork published a report that examines the impact of the growing number of data centres (a critical component of the AI industry) on Ireland’s energy and environmental landscape. The report shows empirical evidence demonstrating the data centre industry as a primary driver of energy usage in Ireland, significantly increasing CO2 emissions as well as other environmental and energy security risks. The report points out policy gaps and relevant recommendations to address them. The organisation has been engaged in broader advocacy work around AI’s environmental impact in Ireland and the EU

Developing ethical guidelines, standards, and best practices

In Argentina, in May 2025, the CIPPEC (Centro de Implementación de Políticas Públicas para la Equidad y el Crecimiento) published the Guía para el uso de IA en el sector público en Argentina, a best-practice guide for AI adoption/use in public agencies. Chapter 7 of the guideline addresses requirements for transparency documentation and explanation across the AI lifecycle – including clear examples and implementation steps to follow.

The general rule is to prioritise prominent organisations recognised for their engagement in AI ethics and governance, those contributing to public debates on the social implications of AI, those engaging in research and knowledge creation, those into policy advocacy or holding government to account, and those providing support for AI-related initiatives. This questionnaire collects evidence across all indicators (primary and secondary) in the Ethics and Sustainability dimension.

Begin by scanning through the webpages of prominent CSOs working on AI in your country. From your search results, look out for other organisations collaborating in this area.

docs.title: Environmental Impact
docs.text:
DefinitionWhy measure this indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • Environmental sustainability refers to the ability to maintain an ecological balance in the planet’s natural environment and conserve natural resources to support the wellbeing of current and future generations.

  • Sustainable AI is an evolving concept that seeks to integrate ecological integrity and social justice throughout the entire AI lifecycle, encompassing idea generation, training, implementation, and governance. This movement advocates for the development of AI systems that go beyond mere application, prioritizing: (i) Environmental stewardship through sustainable use of environmental resources for present and future generations; (ii) Economic sustainability through models that support societies; (iii) and engendering societal values. While Sustainable AI encompasses both AI for sustainability and sustainability of AI development and deployment, this indicator focuses exclusively on the latter, that is, the environmental sustainability of AI development and use.

  • This indicator is grounded in the broader conceptual framework of Sustainable AI, which is composed of two separate, but interrelated parts: (1) AI for sustainability; and (2) sustainability of AI. AI for sustainability refers to the application of AI systems for the purpose of achieving sustainability in some manner, such as for environmental conservation or for the achievement of the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Sustainability of AI refers to sustainability of developing and using AI models, such as extent of carbon footprints, impact of computational power for training algorithms, rising temperatures of cloud storage.

  • The development and use of AI systems pose serious threats to the environment and long-term sustainability of the planet. For example, the Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector is responsible for up to 2.8% of global greenhouse gas emissions; the design and development processes of AI technology in data centres consume high amounts of both energy and water; and the need for new computing resources and information technology (IT) infrastructure is waste-intensive. Moreover, 82.6% of globally-generated e-waste is either incinerated or deposited into landfills; e-waste is projected to reach 75 million metric tons by 2030, the majority of which ends up in countries in the Global South.

  • In response to the environmental risks posed by AI development, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI calls upon member states to incentivise measures that monitor, protect, and support the environment. This includes actions that support sustainable consumption and production patterns, ranging from infrastructure plans to innovative business models, as well as actions that facilitate access to, and use of, sustainable energy in a way that considers its social impact. Similarly, the OECD recommends that policymakers tackle several key areas to address the environmental impact of AI. These include establishing measurement standards for sustainable AI, collecting data on its environmental effects, broadening the scope of environmental impacts considered, and enhancing both environmental transparency and equity. Additionally, the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal, ratified by 190 countries, prohibits the export of e-waste from more economically developed nations to less developed ones.

  • While AI can also be leveraged to promote environmental protection and sustainability in other sectors (“AI for sustainability”), this indicator is limited to assessing the sustainability of AI itself.

  • Accordingly, states must not only assess, but also take measures to mitigate, harmful environmental impacts of AI by reducing the amounts of: carbon emissions generated by AI systems; computing power used to train AI models; and e-waste/unnecessary waste of natural resources. Specifically, AI actors should conduct assessments at each stage of the AI lifecycle and use sustainable power to develop infrastructure that measures and reduces the carbon footprint from training algorithms. Legislative frameworks governing e-waste should strive to reduce its production. To promote positive environmental impact, AI systems can be leveraged to enable more sustainable practices in other sectors and industries, such as architecture (e.g. energy-efficient design); renewable energy (e.g. optimising deployment); as well as in agriculture, textile production, and electronics (e.g. waste management and deforestation monitoring). Because responsible AI demands identifying and acting on any adverse effects and because ethical AI further demands consideration of its social impact, examination of this indicator is necessary.

This indicator examines country mechanisms, such as frameworks and government-led initiatives, that are designed to advance sustainable AI. It specifically looks at efforts to mitigate the long-term adverse environmental impacts of AI. Key areas of assessment for this indicator include:

  • The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste. Examples: (i) encourage the use of smaller, more efficient AI models for everyday tasks, rather than defaulting to large, energy-intensive ones that may only offer marginal performance gains; (ii) establish a repository of pre-trained models so that researchers and developers don't have to start from scratch.

  • The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models. Examples: (i) require AI developers to include a "carbon label" with their models, detailing the estimated energy consumption and carbon emissions generated during training and deployment; (ii) obligate organizations to conduct and publish an environmental impact assessment for any large-scale AI project before it is deployed, outlining the project's projected energy and water usage.

  • The establishment of rights for communities and organizations to be informed about the environmental impact of large-scale AI projects and to advocate for more sustainable practices. Examples: (i) establish a formal process for public consultation before the construction of new data centers, allowing communities to voice concerns and advocate for the use of renewable energy sources and sustainable land use. (ii) enact legislation that gives local communities the legal right to request and receive detailed information about the energy and water consumption of nearby data centers and AI facilities.

  • The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers, including the use of renewable energy sources, advanced cooling technologies, and optimized hardware, to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption. Examples: (i) Provide tax incentives or subsidies for data centers that power their operations with 100% renewable energy, such as solar or wind; (ii) offer grants or financial assistance for data centers to invest in advanced cooling technologies, such as liquid immersion cooling, which can significantly reduce energy consumption and water use compared to traditional air-conditioning systems.

  • Government Frameworks These could be laws, regulations, policies (published or draft form), and/or guidelines. They could recommend or require the government and non-state actors to advance environmental sustainability as it relates to AI. France’s National AI Strategy includes provisions that address the environmental impact of AI in relation to the sustainability of AI. This strategic area calls for the design and development of more environmentally-friendly AI – including the development of more ecological AI infrastructure (e.g. the cloud industry).

  • Government-led Initiatives These could include concrete government actions, projects or programs approved or operational during the study timeframe, funded, and managed by a government entity to address issues of environmental protection and sustainability. The National AI Research Program (NAIRP) and the National Institute for Research in Digital Science and Technology (INRIA) are playing a leading role in the implementation of France’s National AI Strategy, specifically in research and innovation. Along with CNRS (National Centre for Scientific Research) and CEA (French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission), INRIA co-leads the National research programme Artificial intelligence (PEPR IA), which aims to respond to the challenges of sustainability, ecological transition and technological sovereignty. One of the key objectives of the programme is to make AI more sustainable by making frugal AI, which is more energy efficient and data-efficient, more accessible. PEPR AI has launched a call for chairs to scientific excellence in AI, offering AI scientists a four-year opportunity to lead a research program and team in France. One of the key scientific priorities within the PEPR AI framework for this call is Frugal AI, focusing on optimising energy performance and resources for training and using models. In addition, the French Ministry of Ecological Transition partnered with the AI Action Summit, HuggingFace, Data for Good France on the Frugal AI Challenge, which invited participants from academia and industry to submit AI models that were energy-efficient, and adhere to sustainable AI practices. The competition aimed to promote environmental sustainability in AI development, and encourage frugal AI model development by availing datasets and evaluation criteria for others to apply to their projects as they develop technological solutions in alignment with sustainable values

Evidence should specifically address environmental sustainability, aligning with the environmental aspects of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This distinction is important, as many government initiatives may highlight the use of AI for environmental purposes, which falls outside the scope of this indicator. Research should encompass only the sustainability of AI

Additionally, government-led initiatives could involve creating an oversight body to monitor adherence to environmental protections and sustainability in AI, the creation of an expert working group to develop policies or programmes in relation to environmental protection and sustainability of AI, or the allocation of funding to promote advancement of environmental protection and sustainability of AI.

docs.title: Fairness and Non Discrimination
docs.text:
DefinitionWhy measure this indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • Fairness in the context of AI refers to the ethical principle that AI systems should operate without producing biased or discriminatory outcomes. It involves ensuring that an AI system's decisions and performance are not unfairly different across various demographic groups, such as those based on race, gender, or age. Ultimately, the goal is to create AI technologies that promote equitable treatment and avoid perpetuating societal biases.

  • Bias is defined as a prejudice for - or against - an individual or group in a way that is oftentimes unfair. Bias arises from the human tendency to classify people into groups according to certain characteristics (e.g. race, gender, nationality, class, etc.) and different levels of power, status, and resources they generally hold. These classifications can lead to judgments about individuals based on the level of power, status, and resources they are presumed to have based on these characteristics and association with particular groups.

  • Algorithmic bias refers to systematic AI errors causing unfair outcomes, often privileging one group. It stems from underrepresented, incomplete or flawed data reflecting historical inequalities, leading to discriminatory impacts on individuals or groups. This can result in unequal access to opportunities, resources, and information, potentially violating human rights and legitimizing discrimination.

  • Discrimination is treating individuals or groups differently based on age, disability, gender, race, sexuality, or other characteristics. Unfair discrimination is unjustifiable treatment of an individual or group, not aimed at achieving equity or advancing disadvantaged groups. Not all discrimination is unfair; some forms, like preferential treatment for women in STEM, promote equity, while others, like surveillance of political dissidents, perpetuate harm.

  • Freedom from unfair discrimination is a protected aspect of the right to equality, a core principle in international human rights laws. Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states that everyone has the right to all freedoms and rights in the Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, color, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth, or other status.

  • Key instruments include the International Covenant on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICEARD), ensuring equal protection against discrimination (Article 1); the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), upholding civil and political rights and non-discrimination (Article 26); and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), guaranteeing equal access to basic services, infrastructure, and scientific benefits, including digital inclusion (Article 15). Additionally, national frameworks clarify non-discrimination, fairness concepts, and remedies for rights violations.

  • Despite advancements in equality, embedded bias in AI systems threatens to exclude marginalized individuals further from economic, social, and political life. Algorithms trained with biased data or designed non-inclusively can lead to discriminatory outcomes. For instance, the 2018 GenderShades project by MIT’s Media Lab revealed a 34.7% error rate for dark-skinned women in facial recognition systems, compared to 0.8% for light-skinned men. This research revealed deeply rooted biases in the accuracy of facial recognition systems based on race and gender. It also underscored that algorithmic fairness is determined by a range of contextually driven factors.

  • Mitigating AI bias involves understanding its origin, who it harms and benefits, how it appears in data, how it reinforces discrimination, and what redress mechanisms can address algorithmic bias. This understanding clarifies governmental measures to leverage AI's potential while reducing bias and unfair discrimination.

This indicator takes a look at the mechanisms (frameworks and government led initiatives) countries have in place to prevent and mitigate the risk of unfair discrimination posed by biases in the design, development and use of AI. Some key areas this indicator would assess include:

  • The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems, ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups. Examples: (i) Auditing AI credit scoring for racial bias to prevent disadvantaging minority applicants. (ii) Designing AI public service systems, like healthcare scheduling, to prioritize equitable access and avoid reinforcing disparities. (iii) Ensuring AI content recommendation engines don't perpetuate gender stereotypes in job advertisements (e.g., STEM for men, nursing for women), promoting broader career options for all.

  • The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race, ethnicity, gender, religion, age, or other protected characteristics. Examples: (i) Annual audits of AI facial recognition systems to prevent higher error rates for darker skin tones, avoiding misidentification and wrongful arrests. (ii) AI models for criminal risk assessment must use fairness metrics to prevent disproportionately high scores for marginalized communities. (iii) Ban biased historical data, like past discriminatory hiring data, when training AI recruitment models.

  • The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify, measure, and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle, from data collection to deployment. Examples: (i) Mandate bias impact assessments (BIAs) for high-risk AI (e.g., social services, law enforcement) to identify biases pre-deployment; (ii) Require developers to publish "model cards" detailing data, limitations, and bias mitigation; (iii) Implement real-time monitoring of AI systems to detect and correct emerging biases, such as in loan approvals.

  • The establishment of rights for individuals to challenge decisions made by AI systems they believe are unfair or discriminatory, with access to meaningful redress. Examples: (i) Give individuals the right to an explanation that allows individuals to detect and challenge potential bias or discriminatory outcomes such as loan denials due to gender or racial discrimination. clear, understandable explanation for AI system decisions, such as loan application denials; (ii) Implement an accessible appeal process for AI decisions, allowing human reviewers to overturn biased or incorrect automated outcomes; (iii) Ensure that AI discrimination claims lead to appropriate remedies, such as a corrected decision, financial compensation, or other redress; (iv) Mandate regular, public reports on AI-related discrimination cases or bias challenges, to ensure transparency and accountability.

  • Government Frameworks These could be laws, regulations, policies (published or draft form), and/or guidelines. They could recommend or require the government and non-state actors to advance fairness and non-discrimination in the context of AI. For example, Chile’s National Artificial Intelligence Policy emphasizes identifying and mitigating biases in AI systems to protect fundamental rights, especially privacy, data protection, and non-arbitrary discrimination by government entities. It also proposes standards for algorithmic transparency in critical applications, aiming for responsible and ethical AI development that respects human rights and prevents discrimination. Similarly, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) issued "Core Principles and Relevant Promotion Policies for the Application of AI in the Financial Industry" on October 17, 2023. These principles aim to help financial institutions leverage AI benefits while managing risks, ensuring fairness, protecting consumer rights, maintaining security, and fostering sustainable development. Emphasizing fairness and human-centric values, the six core principles guide financial institutions to minimize algorithmic bias in AI systems.

  • Government-led Initiatives These could include concrete government actions, projects or programs approved or operational during the study timeframe, funded, and managed by a government entity to advance fairness and non-discrimination in the context of AI. It may also include the establishment of an oversight body mandated to monitor compliance with principles related to bias and unfair discrimination in AI, the creation of an expert working group to develop policies or programmes in relation to bias and unfair discrimination and AI, or the allocation of funding to promote advancement of bias and unfair discrimination in relation to AI. For example, Uruguay's 2021-2024 Action Plan includes the establishment of an Artificial Intelligence Observatory within the State. This Observatory aims to foster the ethical, responsible, secure, and reliable application of AI technology while bolstering Uruguay's AI ecosystem. Its goals include developing recommendations, criteria, and principles for state AI usage and algorithmic transparency. This will involve incorporating input from various stakeholders and addressing risks such as bias and discrimination.

When reviewing sources, look for terms like 'algorithmic systems,' 'automated systems,' and 'algorithmic/automated decisions,' as they may indicate discussions about AI, bias, non-discrimination, or fairness, even if AI isn't explicitly mentioned. Prioritize evidence that offer measures to reduce bias, unrepresentative datasets, or discriminatory algorithmic outcomes, especially those protecting vulnerable groups, including indigenous communities.

docs.title: Human Oversight and Determination
docs.text:
DefinitionWhy measure this indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • Human oversight in the context of AI refers to the practice of having humans actively monitor, supervise, control, review, and intervene in the operations of an AI system to ensure it's safe, ethical, and aligned with its intended purpose. It is a critical component of responsible AI development and deployment, especially for high-risk systems. Human oversight, as defined by the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI can also encompass 'inclusive public oversight.'

  • The level of human involvement varies depending on the system's risk and purpose. Two common models for human oversight are: (i) Human-in-the-loop (HITL), a hands-on approach where humans are directly involved in every decision the AI makes, especially during the training and validation phases. The AI acts as an assistant, and a human must approve or reject its output before any action is taken. Examples of this are often used in healthcare, where a doctor reviews an AI's diagnosis. (ii) Human-on-the-loop (HOTL), an approach in which humans supervise an AI system's overall performance. While not reviewing every decision, humans are prepared to intervene if the AI system acts unexpectedly or unsafely. This method is often used for highly autonomous systems that still need a human failsafe.

  • Human determination, which is often referred to as ‘human agency’, is defined as ‘the capacity of an individual to act with free will’, which is most clearly demonstrated through the choices people make. Human determination in AI allows individuals to exercise judgment, assess complex ethical considerations, and make informed decisions. This ensures AI aligns with human values and responsible use, taking into account broader societal impacts.

  • This indicator is a vital safeguard against the potential risks of AI systems; the principle of 'human oversight and determination' necessitates human involvement throughout the AI lifecycle, from design and development to use and deployment. This approach aims to achieve several goals, including improving AI performance and safety, upholding ethical principles like legitimacy, accountability, human autonomy, and agency, and building public trust in AI. Specifically, the introduction of policies mandating human oversight and determination acts as a quality control mechanism to prevent algorithmic harms, while also upholding human rights and dignity based on a rights-based approach to AI.

  • The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI requires Member States to ensure that individuals and existing legal entities hold ethical and legal responsibility for AI systems throughout their lifecycle. This broadens the understanding of human oversight to also encompass public oversight. The framework stresses that Member States must ensure individuals retain the power to decide whether to grant control to AI systems in specific situations. It underscores the paramount importance of preserving ultimate human responsibility and accountability, regardless of how much humans rely on AI. While humans might choose to depend on AI systems for efficiency, the ultimate decision to relinquish control rests with them. Consequently, AI systems can never assume or replace human responsibility and accountability for the outcomes or impact of their actions.

  • Some jurisdictions, such as the European Union, present human-in-the-loop and human-in-command as different governance mechanisms for implementing the principle of human oversight and determination. For example, the Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI defines the ‘human in the loop’ as the capability for humans to monitor every stage of the AI lifecycle and assume a supervisory role which can intervene on a needs basis only. This approach carries the benefit of enabling humans to put ‘realistic trust’ into the system in a way while also preserving the quality of the system performance.

This indicator measures mechanisms (frameworks and government led initiatives) countries have taken to promote and facilitate human oversight and determination of AI systems, and to ensure a certain degree of human control in the design and operation of AI systems. Some key areas this indicator would assess include:

  • The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems, ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment, particularly in critical areas, where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications. Examples: mandate the use of AI tools for high stake applications, which have significant potential risks to lives and livelihoods, or directly impact vulnerable and at-risk communities, to require human authorization before any action is taken.

  • The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary, such as in law enforcement or medicine. Examples: (i) A ban on the development and deployment of fully autonomous weapons systems that can select and engage targets without human intervention, as their use would bypass fundamental ethical and legal principles of war. (ii) require that all parole and sentencing recommendations made by AI systems be subject to mandatory review by a judge or a human review board.

  • The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee, intervene in, and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system. Examples: (i) require organizations that deploy AI in high-stakes areas, such as financial trading, to appoint a designated AI officer who is legally and ethically accountable for any market manipulation or instability caused by their automated systems. (ii) obligate companies to provide comprehensive training for all employees who interact with AI systems, ensuring they understand the system's limitations and know when human intervention is necessary.

  • The establishment of rights for individuals to have an opportunity for human review and appeal of decisions made by an AI system, ensuring that the final say rests with a person. Examples: (i) grant individuals the right to have a decision made by an AI system (e.g., denial of a social security benefit) reviewed by a human caseworker who can consider the case on its merits and override the automated outcome; (ii) provide a formal and accessible process for individuals to appeal a decision made by an AI, such as a university admissions decision based on an AI-powered screening tool; (iii) establish an independent board to review AI-driven decisions that are challenged by individuals, with the power to reverse outcomes and issue recommendations for improving the AI system's fairness.

  • Government Frameworks These could be laws, regulations, policies (published or draft form), and/or guidelines. They could recommend or require the government and non-state actors to promote meaningful human control or prevent full automation in sensitive sectors. For example, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s 2023 AI Ethics Principles emphasize two key principles: the periodic monitoring and control of AI systems to ensure their operations and functionalities align with their design, and the necessity of human oversight in these processes. It also outlines the need for designing and developing AI systems that can withstand various uncertainties is crucial, requiring both inherent oversight capabilities and intervention tools. Additionally, it highlights the need to involve all parties throughout the AI system's lifecycle is essential to ensure the system's representativeness, reliability, and relevance.

  • Government-led Initiatives These could include concrete government actions, projects or programs approved or operational during the study timeframe, funded, and managed by a government entity to advance human oversight and determination. It may also include the establishment of an oversight body mandated to monitor compliance with principles related to the indicator, the creation of an expert working group to develop policies or programmes. For example, Estonia's AI governance aligns with European regulatory frameworks, including the GDPR, which emphasises human oversight. The country’s courts use 'Salme', an AI-powered speech recognition assistant, to transcribe court proceedings. This nationwide system records hearings and creates transcripts, with operators manually identifying attendees before each session. Court clerks provide this oversight by reviewing and correcting the AI-generated text as needed. Estonia has also introduced a semi-automated system for small claims in civil proceedings. This system uses algorithms to generate payment orders automatically, based on information provided by the involved parties. Human oversight is still maintained for critical functions like establishing jurisdiction and ensuring proper document service.

When reviewing evidence/sources, look for terms like ‘human intervention’, ‘human control’, human-centric’, ‘human-in-the-loop’, ‘human-on-the-loop’, ‘human-in-command’. In terms of government frameworks, specific reference should be made to the principle of human oversight and determination or one of the terms mentioned above. It is important to note that frameworks may provide a requirement for, or otherwise describe or emphasise the importance of, instituting some degree of human control or oversight, without detailing any specific mechanisms or minimum requirements. In terms of government-led initiatives, look for evidence of government initiatives to advance principles of human oversight and determination in the design and roll-out of AI systems, which may include the development of draft policies or the establishment of an expert working group to explore the concept of ‘human-in-the-loop’.

docs.title: Transparency and Explainability
docs.text:
DefinitionWhy measure this indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • Transparency is defined as ‘the quality of [a process, practice or decision] being done in an open way without secrets so people can trust that [actions] are fair and honest’. Transparency has been identified by the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) as one of the five key principles of good governance, along with responsibility, accountability, participation and responsiveness to public concerns.

  • AI transparency refers to the degree of accessibility and openness of an AI system's internal mechanisms, necessitating the provision of comprehensible explanations of algorithms, models, datasets, and rationale for their use. It also refers to transparency in their capabilities and use whether by a public or private actor to ensure that people understand these systems, including the reasons for their development, training, deployment, and impact.

  • Accordingly, the principle of transparency implies the concept of explainability, which refers to ‘the quality of enabling people to understand how a particular system works and/or how a particular outcome was achieved by providing information that is sensible and easy-to-understand’. The principle of explainability is also closely linked to the concept of interpretability, which refers to ‘the capacity to provide an explanation of the factors and logic that led to an outcome in terms that are understandable to a human.’ Transparency and explainability, as principles of responsible AI governance, therefore require information about processes, practices and decisions to be open, accessible, and easily understood by a broad range of stakeholders, including government entities, private sector companies, civil society organisations and academic institutions.

  • Given AI's growing role in predictions, recommendations, and decisions, transparency regarding its use, functionality, and impact is vital. Understanding AI's reasoning, deployment, processes, and training data is crucial due to potential risks. As shown in the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, a lack of transparency can hinder the ability to challenge AI-based decisions, affecting fair trials and access to redress. Conversely, increased transparency allows individuals to understand AI system operations, identify influencing factors, and verify the presence of safeguards like safety and fairness measures.

  • The OECD states that transparency in AI requires disclosing how AI systems are used, especially when making predictions or recommendations, or when people interact with AI agents. This involves providing easily understandable information on AI system development, training, operation, and deployment, enabling informed decisions. Additionally, the OECD emphasizes the importance of open dialogue among stakeholders and dedicated entities to raise AI awareness, address public concerns, and build confidence in responsible AI application.

This indicator measures mechanisms (frameworks and government led initiatives) countries have taken to promote and ensure sufficient levels of transparency and explainability in the development, use and deployment of AI technologies. Some key areas this indicator would assess include

  • The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate, including their purpose, data sources, and decision-making logic, to foster public trust. Examples: (i) Public register of high-risk AI systems, detailing purpose, training data, and performance metrics; (ii) insisting that user-facing AI tools (e.g., medical diagnostics) must summarize influencing factors like symptoms or lab results; (iii) Promoting open-source AI for public and research scrutiny of code and logic.

  • The prevention of "black box" AI where the internal workings are opaque, making it difficult to understand how and why a decision was reached. Examples: (i) Mandatory explainability standards; (ii) requiring independent third-party audits of AI systems to verify their decision-making processes; and (iii) prohibiting the use of highly complex, unexplainable AI models in contexts where their decisions could have a significant impact on an individual's life, such as in child welfare risk assessments.

  • The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs, especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications. Examples: (i) Obligate financial institutions to provide a clear, easy-to-understand explanation to loan applicants if their application is denied by an AI system, detailing the key factors that contributed to the decision; (ii) Require employers to explicitly inform job candidates if an AI system is being used to screen their resumes or conduct initial interviews; (iii) Mandate that companies using AI in areas like content moderation publish regular transparency reports detailing how their AI systems operate and the types of content they remove.

  • The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them, and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome. Examples: (i) Grant individuals the right to request the specific data points an AI system used to make a decision about them, such as a credit score report; (ii) Implement a user-friendly process where individuals can automatically request and receive an explanation for a decision; (iii) Guarantee an individual's right to appeal an AI-driven decision and have it reviewed by a human who can access the explanation provided by the AI and make an independent judgment.

  • Government Frameworks These could be laws, regulations, policies (published or draft form), and/or guidelines. They could recommend or require the government and non-state actors to advance transparency and explainability in AI. Start by identifying any binding law or regulation that aims to govern AI. Note the different terms often synonymous with transparency regarding AI such as ‘notice’, ‘disclosure’, and ‘black box’. Look for evidence of specific regulatory requirements that call for notice requirements or specific policy recommendations in relation to transparency. Transparency requirements may be proportional to perceived risk levels. AI systems may also be referred to as ‘algorithmic systems’, and it may be useful to include ‘machine learning’ in searches. For example, New Zealand enforces AI transparency and explainability through frameworks like the Artificial Intelligence and Information Privacy Principles (IPP). IPP, for example, requires agencies to disclose collected information and its usage, applying to AI by mandating understanding of training data and development processes. For AI tools screening documents, transparency is crucial before reliance.

  • Government-led Initiatives These could include concrete government actions, projects or programs approved or operational during the study timeframe, funded, and managed by a government entity to advance transparency and explainability in the context of AI. It may also include the establishment of an oversight body mandated to monitor compliance with principles related to the indicator, the creation of an expert working group to develop policies or programmes. Ireland established a national AI Advisory Council in January 2024 to provide independent expert advice to the government on artificial intelligence policy. The AI Advisory Council is delegated to provide expert insights advisory to the government on emerging opportunities and challenges regarding AI, as well as engaging in public relations to promote trustworthy, ethical and human-centred AI. To foster public trust in AI, the Council recommends that the government adopt responsible AI innovation, stressing the importance of public transparency and accountability, including implementing legislative and accountability frameworks to ensure accurate, fair, and transparent AI applications, as well as regular independent auditing particularly for technologies such as facial recognition.

When reviewing sources, look for terms like 'algorithmic systems,' 'automated systems,' and 'algorithmic/automated decisions,' as they may indicate discussions about transparency and explainability, even if AI isn't explicitly mentioned. Search the responsible ministry website (e.g. Ministry of Economics, Ministry of Technology, Ministry of Justice, etc.) and identify events, monitoring mechanisms or information related to transparency and explainability. Check if there might be guidelines specifying the application of general laws (consumer protection etc.) to the use-case of AI that impose specific notice requirements or dissemination specifications to ensure adequate explainability.

docs.title: Children's Rights
docs.text:
DefinitionsWhy measure this indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • Children’s rights refer to the subset of human rights that recognises the need to provide children with special care and protection given their dependence on adults for survival, protection, and development. A ‘child’ is defined as anyone under the age of 18, or until they attain majority, or legal age, earlier under an applicable law.

  • The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) recognises the primary role of parents in safeguarding the rights of their children, it also places affirmative obligations on states to create the conditions for these responsibilities to be fulfilled. The UNCRC sets the global standard for children’s rights which can be broadly organised into four categories: (i) Survival rights which include the right to life and access to basic services such as food, shelter, adequate living standards, and medical services. (ii) Development rights which include the right to education, play, leisure, cultural activities, access to information, and freedom of thought, conscience and religion.(iii) Protection rights which include the right to be protected from all forms of abuse, neglect and exploitation. (iv) Participation rights which include the right to freedom of expression, to have a say in matters affecting their lives, and to join associations and to assemble peacefully.

  • In 2021, the UN’s Committee on the Rights of the Child published General Comment No. 25 on ‘children’s rights in relation to the digital environment’, guiding states on implementing the UNCRC digitally. Similarly, UNICEF’s AI for children project developed policy guidance on AI for children, based on the UNCRC, recommending how states and organizations can uphold children’s rights in AI policy and systems.

  • Various human rights instruments protect children's rights in the digital age, including AI contexts. These include the UN's Optional Protocol on the sale of children, child prostitution, and child pornography; the Council of Europe's Convention on the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse; and the OECD's Recommendation of the Council on Children in the Digital Environment and Guidelines for Digital Service Providers. The African Union Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy is another relevant non-binding instrument. While not specific to artificial intelligence, these instruments establish important protections for children in digital environments, including AI systems.

  • AI is increasingly present in children's daily lives, powering social media, apps, websites, and online games that offer recommendations and mediate content. Similarly, there have been recent emergence of AI-enhanced toys, designed to provide interactive and personalised play experience. While potentially beneficial, unregulated AI use poses risks to children's rights to privacy, play, protection from exploitation and abuse, and non-discrimination due to a lack of transparency. Children are also more vulnerable to harmful content and advertising in the digital environment.

  • A 2020 analysis of national strategies on protecting children online found that while some countries had legislative and policy responses, they were often "fragmented" and lacked a "comprehensive framework" or coordinated government response. Many countries face the challenge of promoting digital media use among youth while protecting them from risks. Government actions (or inaction) disproportionately affect children, making this area essential for assessing responsible AI.

This indicator examines the measures countries have in place and/or are developing to ensure that the design, development and use of AI is happening in a way that upholds children’s rights. Some key areas this indicator would assess include:

  • The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems. Examples: requirements to anonymise and encrypt children’s data.

  • The prevention of the use of AI to exploit, manipulate, or harm children, including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content. Examples: implementation of security measures including transparency about data use, restrictions around third-party sharing of children’s data.

  • The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe, age-appropriate, and beneficial for children. Examples: requirements for developers designing AI tools for children, guardians and schools to perform child-specific risk assessments.

  • The establishment of rights for children, and their guardians, to seek redress if they are harmed by AI systems. Examples: requirements for child-accessible harm reporting mechanisms, prioritisation of addressing AI-related harms related to children, and legal remedies of AI-enabled harms toward children

  • Government Frameworks These could be laws, regulations, policies (published or draft form), and/or guidelines. They could recommend or commit the government and non-state actors to protect children's rights from AI risks. These may be standalone or integrated into existing digital human rights frameworks. For example, Scotland's 2021 AI Strategy acknowledges AI's impact on children and aims to establish policies empowering them in AI development and use. Particularly, the strategy outlines key principles for children and AI: protecting data and privacy, ensuring safety, providing transparency and accountability, educating governments and businesses on AI's impact on children's rights, and fostering child-centered AI. Similarly, the Portuguese Charter of the Human Rights in the Digital Age grants children the right to protection and special care, including safety in cyberspace and freedom of expression, all applicable to AI and its impact.The Charter specifically addresses the rights of children, including their entitlement to special protection and care for their well-being and safety in cyberspace as well as their rights to freedom of expression of information or ideas commensurate with their age and maturity. These rights, as stated in the Charter, extend to AI-related issues, particularly concerning its potential impact on children.

  • Government-led Initiatives These could include concrete government actions, projects or programs approved or operational during the study timeframe, funded, and managed by a government entity to protect and / or promote children’s rights in the context of AI. It can be implemented by the government or in collaboration with other organizations, such as non-profits, private companies, or other countries. For this indicator, some examples include the United Kindgdom, which has collaborated with the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, to actively combat online child sexual abuse, including cases involving AI. The country is working with its partners to develop advanced tools to identify AI-generated material and minimise law enforcement exposure to child sexual abuse images by using AI to the UK's child abuse image database. It has also engaged with tech companies supporting voluntary principles to counter online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

We recommend focusing on frameworks and measures that address rights specific to children in the context of AI. This includes a range of protections, such as their right to privacy and data protection, which encompasses the right not to be subjected to undue surveillance. It also extends to ensuring their safety from abuse and harm when interacting with AI, particularly on social media. This necessitates that children and their caregivers are included in the development of AI governance systems. Examine country policies/guidelines and measures to mitigate risks to children's rights and leverage benefits, and government actions (programs, interventions, monitoring/oversight) to implement them. If references to the latter but not the former exist, note this gap. Look for direct mentions of children's rights frameworks like the UNCRC and others mentioned above, and implementation measures. State-level frameworks might require private firms to meet data standards for children, offer remedies for violations (e.g., statutory liability for AI harm), or run awareness campaigns.

docs.title: CSO Engagement on Inclusion and Diversity
docs.text:
DefinitionWhy Measure this Indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • To safeguard people's rights effectively, active civic participation is essential in ensuring accountability, amplifying marginalised voices, and representing the public interest in AI governance processes. In this regard, civil society organisations (CSOs) working in the field of artificial intelligence play a crucial role in actively shaping policies, implementing projects, raising public awareness, lobbying for policy formulation and implementation, and holding the government to account.

  • According to the United Nations, “a civil society organisation (CSO) or non-governmental organisation (NGO) is any non-profit, voluntary citizens’ group which is organised on a local, national or international level”. These organisations focus on specific issues of public interest, such as human rights, poverty alleviation, inclusion, and inequality. The EU notes that “civil society refers to all forms of social action carried out by individuals or groups who are neither connected to nor managed by state authorities”, while CSOs are institutionalised or formal organisations “whose members serve the general interest through a democratic process and which plays the role of mediator between public authorities and citizens”.

  • CSOs operate through a variety of structures, including as charities, faith-based organisations, think tanks and research centres, trade unions, community groups, online networks, and social and recreational clubs. In the AI context, the defining quality for a CSO is that the non-profit organisation engages in policy influencing, public awareness, research, knowledge production, advisory, advocacy or any other activity geared towards responsible development and deployment of AI.

CSOs play a critical, sometimes outsized role, in advancing responsible AI practices and policies. Data from the 2024 edition of the Global Index on Responsible AI identified more than 400 CSOs working to advance responsible AI across 19 thematic areas including gender equality, children's rights, and cultural and linguistic diversity. Evidence of CSO engagement in these areas fill a crucial gap and offer a holistic assessment of the responsible AI ecosystem globally, given that in some contexts — such as Africa — CSO activities often surpass government-led efforts in responsible AI.

The questionnaire for this indicator asks researchers to document evidence of CSO activities across all indicators (primary and secondary) in the Inclusion and Diversity dimension: Gender Equality, Children’s Rights, Cultural and Linguistic Diversity, and Rights of Persons with Disability. Researchers should therefore consider both the breadth of the evidence of initiatives as well as how well such evidence covers all the indicators. There are 6 CSO initiative types in the questionnaire:

  • Participation in public policy formulation, implementation, M\&E: as part of advisory councils, partnerships with state, independent observers, participating in parliamentary hearings
  • Litigation or legal action.
  • Capacity building and collaboration
  • Public engagement & awareness: conferences, public awareness events/campaigns, public consultations
  • Knowledge generation: research, technical reports.
  • Developing ethical guidelines, standards, and best practices

You are to provide one evidence per initiative type and indicate which indicator(s) the evidence covers. It is very likely that initiatives are more concentrated on one indicator than others – this is fine, but we encourage researchers to ensure, where evidence is available, that each indicator has at least one evidence of a CSO initiative addressing it. Initiatives must be either ongoing or have taken place during the study timeframe (November 1, 2023 – September 30, 2025).

You should only provide evidence that shows country-level engagement of CSO initiatives. Evidence from international CSOs are relevant, only if the initiative addresses your country's context and actual participation in the initiative from local partners could be demonstrated — this includes country chapters of international CSOs. For example, a report by the Center for Democracy and Technology on the impact of algorithmic hiring tools on PWD applicants does not highlight any country context and would not count in this regard.

Examples below are provided by initiative type:

Participation in public policy formulation, implementation, M\&E: as part of advisory councils, partnerships with state, independent observers, participating in parliamentary hearings:

In December 2024, in the UK, 5Rights Foundation, a non-profit organisation working on protecting the rights of children in the digital space, submitted written evidence to the Science, Innovation and Technology Select Committee of the UK Parliament in response to the Committee’s call for evidence on the role that social media played in spreading misinformation during the UK 2024 riots, leading to the arrest of many — including some children. Being an organisation that works primarily on children, the 5Rights Foundation submitted written evidence addressing how social media algorithms fuel such misinformation. One of the areas 5Rights Foundation addressed include discussing the roles that generative AI and LLMs play in creating and spreading harmful content and misinformation, including citing examples of AI-generated Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) on social media platforms.

Litigation or legal action

In October 2024, in France, about 15 NGOs which include La Quadrature du Net, Amnesty International France, the Abbé Pierre Foundation, and the Human Rights League, have filed a lawsuit against CNAF — the French government agency responsible for the administration of family-oriented social security system — asking for the agency to pause its use of social scoring algorithms due to concerns about widely known discriminatory practices against disabled people and single mothers.

Capacity building and collaboration

In October 2022, in the UK, the Alan Turing Institute, together with the Scottish-based Children’s Parliament and Scottish AI Alliance (SAIA), launched a three-phased, two-year-project called ‘Exploring Children’s Rights in AI’ to investigate the relationship between primary school learners and AI. The project has hosted workshops in schools where basic concepts around AI and children’s human rights were taught and children’s voices were heard, in support of the non-discrimination principle with regard to children and AI. The Institute hosted the Children’s AI Summit in April 2025, where the Children’s Manifesto for the Future of AI was developed and later presented at the Paris Action Summit.

Public engagement & awareness: conferences, public awareness events/campaigns, public consultations:

In Uganda, Pollicy, a non-profit organisation works to integrate AI into the larger feminist movement by promoting suitable data governance practices and advocating for responsible policies by engaging with women’s groups and gender minorities.

Knowledge generation: research, technical reports.

In April 2025, the National Academy of Social Insurance, a non-profit organisation, composed of social insurance professionals in the US, published a report titled “Task Force on Artificial Intelligence, Emerging Technology, and Disability Benefits”. The report was the product of a taskforce earlier set up to examine the Social Security Administration (US government agency)’s approaches to /use of AI in social security insurance and other schemes for PWDs. The report outlines risks with using AI in such administration, the current state of play in the use of algorithms for determining benefits for PWDs, and principles or guardrails to prevent harms.

Developing ethical guidelines, standards, and best practices

The American Foundation for the Blind has published a set of guiding principles toward development and deployment of more disability inclusive AI systems. The document discusses these rights in the USA context, where the Foundation operates — based on inputs from government, industry, civil society, and academic experts. The document, though published in February 2025, is hosted as a set of live principles (relevant beyond publication date) on the AFB’s website.

The general rule is to prioritise prominent organisations recognised for their engagement in AI ethics and governance, those contributing to public debates on the social implications of AI, those engaging in research and knowledge creation, those into policy advocacy or holding government to account, and those providing support for AI-related initiatives. This questionnaire collects evidence across all indicators (primary and secondary) in the Inclusion and Diversity dimension.

Begin by scanning through the webpages of prominent CSOs working on AI in your country. From your search results, look out for other organisations collaborating in this area.

docs.title: Cultural and Linguistic Diversity
docs.text:
DefinitionsWhy measure this indicator?What to look out forExamplesResearch Guidance

  • Cultural diversity refers to the range of ideas, customs and social behaviors shared by different groups of people in time and place, often expressed through language. It is an integral ‘source of exchange, innovation and creativity’ which promotes the achievement of ‘a more satisfactory intellectual, emotional, moral and spiritual existence’ for all citizens. According to UNESCO, ‘[t]he defense of cultural diversity is an ethical imperative, inseparable from respect for human dignity’ and accordingly ‘implies a commitment to human rights and fundamental freedoms,’ including those of minorities and/or indigenous persons. Similarly, Article 3 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) calls on State Parties to ensure equal access ‘to the enjoyment of all economic, social and cultural rights’ set forth in the Covenant.

  • Additionally, cultural and linguistic diversity is an underpinning value of responsible AI and may be advanced through the active participation of all groups regardless of race, color, descent, gender, age, language, religion, political opinion, national origin, ethnic origin, social origin, economic or social condition of birth, or disability, or any other ground.

  • When AI is developed within specific cultural and linguistic contexts that do not adequately represent the diversity of global cultures where it is deployed, it can lead to cultural biases. These biases raise ethical concerns and perpetuate prejudices. AI systems developed by people of similar cultural groups and used in diverse cultural settings, can lead to discrimination and harm for cultural minorities, including indigenous groups. Significantly, too, AI systems reflecting dominant cultural norms and languages may contribute to the erosion of local cultural diversity, and the suppression of minority languages

  • The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI urges member states to promote and preserve cultural diversity and mitigate risks of its exclusion in AI design and development. This includes examining the impact on local languages through the use of AI systems such as natural language processing (NLP) applications and to take measures to preserve ‘endangered languages, local dialects, and tonal and cultural variations’ associated with indigenous persons and their expression.

  • Assessing state measures to decolonize AI requires a focus on cultural diversity. Historically, Western society's presumed objectivity has marginalized traditional cultural values and knowledge systems across the Global Majority. When these assumptions are embedded in AI design, they can perpetuate biases, leading to discriminatory outcomes in communities where AI systems are deployed. For instance, the lack of natural language processing capabilities in local languages within AI datasets or throughout the AI lifecycle can reproduce historical harms against marginalized groups, increasing exclusion and underrepresentation. Furthermore, if AI is not developed with due regard for local cultures, risks, and needs, alongside an understanding of local value systems, it may reproduce the historical appropriation, extraction, and/or monetization of traditional cultural knowledge systems.

  • To mitigate potential harms, states and AI actors should increase cultural diversity within the AI workforce, as current AI processes are often shaped by individuals with similar backgrounds and hegemonic worldviews. Additionally, investment in local AI development is crucial. Conversely, measures can be taken to leverage AI for the protection of local and indigenous cultures and knowledge systems.

This indicator examines the measures countries have in place to promote and protect cultural diversity in the design, development and use of AI. Some key areas this indicator would assess include:

  • The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages. Examples: engaging multicultural and multilingual groups’ in AI systems’ training and development processes

  • The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes, erase linguistic diversity, or favor dominant cultures. Examples: mandating ethical AI development audits that particularly assess fair and equitable representation of diverse cultural and linguistic groups

  • The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts. Examples: requirements for using diverse and representative datasets for training AI systems, particularly for high-risk domains and active engagement of affected community members in AI development

  • The establishment of rights to redress for individuals and communities harmed by AI systems that misrepresent or discriminate against their cultural or linguistic identities. Examples: enforcement of accountability frameworks for discriminatory outcomes against cultural or linguistic identities from AI systems, designation of independent oversight bodies to respond to AI-related complaints and streamline commensurate redress mechanisms

  • The promotion of AI systems that, by design, promote and preserve cultural heritage and/or cultural minorities, including endangered languages and indigenous languages and knowledge. Examples: funding AI research and projects for underrepresented languages, dedicated national projects or initiatives targeted toward cultural and linguistic preservation, particularly for endangered cultures and languages.

  • Evaluating and addressing the impact of AI systems on local cultural diversity, particularly the effects of natural language processing (NLP) applications like automated translation and voice assistants—on the nuances of human language, expression, and minority languages. Examples: mandates for impact assessments of AI language technologies and commitments to address potential negative implications on underrepresented languages and communities

  • The enhancement of cultural and linguistic diversity in the AI workforce. Examples: mentorship programs to support AI workers underrepresented cultural groups and linguistic communities, enforcing anti-discrimination and inclusive hiring protocols in the AI workforce.

  • Government Frameworks These could be laws, regulations, policies (published or draft form), and/or guidelines. They could recommend or commit the government and non-state actors to advance cultural and linguistic diversity in the context of AI. Egypt's 2019 National AI Strategy is addressing the risk of cultural and linguistic nuance loss in AI, by developing a plan to launch five pilot projects that integrate culture into NLP. Similarly, Slovenia's 2025 National Program to Promote the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence highlights the importance of fostering AI development in the national language. This program recognizes that English-language dominated digitalization can threaten the use of national languages, which are crucial for cultural identity. Furthermore, the policy underscores AI's potential in safeguarding cultural heritage and archival materials.

  • Government-led Initiatives These could include concrete government actions, projects or programs approved or operational during the study timeframe, funded, and managed by a government entity to protect and / or promote linguistic and cultural diversity in AI. Egypt has launched an Applied Innovation Center (AIC) with the aim of: (1) building national capacity in AI; and (2) developing a series of innovative AI projects that can be used to address a range of societal issues across a range of priority sectors. Part of this involves the AIC collaborating with tech vendors to develop ‘leading-edge systems for machine translation, text to speech synthesis, and automatic speech recognition for colloquial Arabic’.

The ways in which cultural diversity may be addressed, include (a) the development of AI in locally/culturally relevant and responsive ways; (b) the empowerment of cultural individual/group actors to use AI to promote cultural diversity; (c) investment in the local development of AI and measures to promote cultural diversity in AI; and (d) implementation of meaningful processes by which impacted communities, including cultural minorities, have the agency to make decisions throughout the AI lifecycle. You may also examine the particular AI application of ‘natural language processing’ in searches that combine the term with ‘culture’, ‘representation’, ‘representativity’ and/or ‘localisation’.
